title: U.S. Thanksgiving Traditions: What Americans Eat, Watch, Do
summary: Explore U.S. Thanksgiving traditions, from turkey and the Macy's parade to football, Friendsgiving, and the dishes families bring to the table.
body_markdown:
***Quick answer:** Common Thanksgiving traditions in the U.S. include sharing a meal with family or friends, pausing to give thanks, and watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade or football. Turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and pumpkin pie are familiar favorites, though many families add their own recipes to the table. Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday in November each year. In 2026, that’s Thursday, November 26.*


**Roast turkey and mashed potatoes sit at one end of the table, scallion pancakes and grilled duck at the other. For many Chinese American families, that combination is what makes Thanksgiving feel complete.**


**That table is one version of an American tradition that looks different in nearly every home. The parade and the football games are familiar to almost everyone, but the guest list, the menu, and even the meaning of the day shift from household to household, shaped by family history, culture, and who is gathered around the table that year.**


**For anyone new to the U.S. or simply curious how the holiday plays out across the country, here is a closer look at what Americans actually do on Thanksgiving, where those customs came from, and how families keep their own traditions alive even when they are an ocean apart.**


## What do Americans do on Thanksgiving?


### Sharing the meal together


At the center of almost every Thanksgiving is a shared meal. One person often takes on the role of host, handling the turkey and the big logistical questions, while guests bring side dishes, bread, or dessert. In many homes, someone suggests going around the table so each person can name one thing they’re grateful for before anyone picks up a fork. It’s a small ritual, but it tends to set the tone for the rest of the day.


### Watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade


Giant character balloons, elaborate floats, and live performances fill the streets of New York City every Thanksgiving morning. The parade began in 1924 as the Macy’s Christmas Parade, organized by store employees as a way to draw holiday shoppers. Over the following decades it grew into the broadcast spectacle millions of households tune into before dinner. You can read more in this[History of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade](https://guides.loc.gov/this-month-in-business-history/november/macys-thanksgiving-parade) .


### Watching or playing football


Football has been tied to Thanksgiving almost as long as the NFL has existed, with games played on the holiday since the league’s founding in 1920. The tradition became an annual fixture in 1934, when then-Detroit Lions owner George A. Richards scheduled a Thanksgiving Day matchup against the Chicago Bears to boost sagging attendance. The Dallas Cowboys joined the tradition in 1966, after general manager Tex Schramm bet that a Thanksgiving slot would raise the team’s profile — a bet that paid off well enough that the Cowboys are still playing on Thanksgiving today. Learn more about[The NFL’s Thanksgiving football tradition](https://www.nfl.com/news/why-do-we-play-on-thanksgiving-day) .


### Celebrating Friendsgiving


Not every Thanksgiving-season gathering happens with family. Friendsgiving describes a Thanksgiving-style meal, usually potluck-style, shared with friends around the holiday. The custom itself may be centuries old, but the word only entered Merriam-Webster’s dictionary in 2020, according to NPR. A typical Friendsgiving might have one friend hosting and handling the turkey, while everyone else splits the sides, drinks, and dessert — a lower-pressure way to celebrate before or after the main event with family.


### Giving back


For many Americans, Thanksgiving is also a moment to think beyond their own table. Some donate food to local pantries in the weeks leading up to the holiday, while others sign up to help serve a community meal. These gestures vary widely from one community to the next, but they share the same spirit: making sure the holiday’s sense of gratitude extends to neighbors who need it most.


## What foods are traditionally served at Thanksgiving?


Most Americans recognize the classic Thanksgiving spread: roast turkey, stuffing or dressing, mashed potatoes with gravy, cranberry sauce, and pumpkin pie.[According to Plimoth Patuxet Museums](https://plimoth.org/yath/unit-4/what-did-they-eat-at-the-1621-harvest-celebration) , this menu developed gradually over centuries — and much about what was actually served at the first harvest gathering in 1621 remains undocumented.


## Where did U.S. Thanksgiving traditions come from?


### The 1621 harvest gathering


The story most Americans learn traces back to a three-day harvest gathering near what is now Plymouth, Massachusetts, shared by English colonists and the Wampanoag. According to the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian, Ousamequin and colonial leader John Carver had reached a treaty of mutual protection months earlier, in the spring of 1621, after careful negotiation — a diplomatic relationship that shaped what followed. The only surviving eyewitness account mentions wildfowl and venison; the rest of the menu remains unknown. For a fuller picture, see these[Wampanoag perspectives on the 1621 harvest gathering](https://americanindian.si.edu/nk360/Thanksgiving/sq4ss1.html) .


### Becoming a federal holiday


Thanksgiving’s path to becoming an official holiday took more than a century. President George Washington proclaimed a day of thanks on October 3, 1789, naming Thursday, November 26, 1789, as the date. President Abraham Lincoln went further in 1863, declaring a nationwide Thanksgiving observance on the last Thursday of November. In 1939, President Franklin D. Roosevelt moved the date up a week to extend the Christmas shopping season, a decision that sparked a national debate. Congress settled the matter in 1941, passing a joint resolution that set Thanksgiving permanently on the fourth Thursday in November. Read more about[how Thanksgiving became a federal holiday](https://www.archives.gov/press/press-releases/2017/nr17-13) .


### The National Day of Mourning


Not every American observes Thanksgiving as a celebration. Since 1970, the United American Indians of New England has organized a National Day of Mourning each Thanksgiving, gathering at noon on Cole’s Hill in Plymouth. According to the organizers, the observance honors Indigenous ancestors and resilience while serving as a day of remembrance and protest against the ongoing effects of colonization. Many Native people choose not to celebrate the arrival of the Pilgrims for this reason. You can learn more directly from[United American Indians of New England](https://uaine.org/) .


## How families keep Thanksgiving traditions across borders


**For families separated by distance, Thanksgiving can take some creativity to feel whole. Some cook the same family recipe in two kitchens at once, comparing notes over video call while both households prepare dinner. Others bring a dish from home to a Friendsgiving potluck, introducing new flavors to friends who’ve never tried them. None of these approaches require getting everything exactly right — they just need to feel like home.**

## Frequently asked questions about U.S. Thanksgiving traditions


### When is Thanksgiving in the U.S. in 2026?


Thanksgiving falls on Thursday, November 26, 2026. The holiday is always observed on the fourth Thursday in November, according to the[U.S. federal holiday schedule](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/pay-leave/federal-holidays/) .


### What is the difference between Thanksgiving and Friendsgiving?


Thanksgiving is the official federal holiday, always held on the fourth Thursday in November. Friendsgiving is an informal, Thanksgiving-style meal that friends organize around the same time of year, usually on whichever day works best for the group.


### Was turkey served at the 1621 harvest gathering?


The only surviving eyewitness account from 1621 mentions wildfowl and venison but doesn’t specify which birds were served. Turkey is possible, but the full menu from that gathering remains unknown.
